title: Hello, Traffic
briefing: Your startup's API just launched. Traffic starts at 100 requests per second and climbs to 350 within 30 seconds.
Every request needs 10ms of CPU time. An app server works on one request per vCPU at a time; the rest wait in line.
Choose one app server that keeps p99 latency under 75ms without going over budget.
debrief: A server with 4 vCPUs and 10ms of CPU per request can handle 400 requests per second. At 350 it isn't overloaded, but it's 87% busy, so most requests arrive while every vCPU is taken and have to wait in line.

Queueing delay grows roughly with 1 / (1 − utilization). Going from 50% to 90% busy multiplies the wait by about five, and close to 100% it explodes. That's why production systems usually aim for 60–70% utilization at peak, not 100%.

Buying a bigger machine is called scaling up, or vertical scaling. It's the simplest fix, but there's always a largest machine, and bigger machines cost proportionally more. The next level hits that ceiling.

solutions.name: One large server
solutions.explanation: 8 vCPUs give 800 req/s of capacity, so 350 req/s keeps it about 44% busy. Requests rarely wait for a free vCPU, so p99 stays close to the raw processing time.

antiSolutions.name: One small server
antiSolutions.explanation: 2 vCPUs handle 200 req/s. At 350 req/s the queue grows without limit and requests time out.

antiSolutions.name: One medium server
antiSolutions.explanation: 400 req/s of capacity is enough to serve every request, but at 87% utilization requests spend too long waiting for a free vCPU.

antiSolutions.name: One xlarge server
antiSolutions.explanation: Fast, but twice the capacity you need at twice the price.
